Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify patients with lumbar stenosis based on history and physical examination findings.
Perform an appropriate clinical evaluation of patients in whom lumbar stenosis is suspected.
Outline appropriate nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for patients with lumbar stenosis.
Overview
Lumbar spine stenosis is the most common reason patients older than 65 years undergo lumbar spine
surgery.
The canal may be narrowed by bony structures (ie, osteophytosis, spondylolisthesis) or soft-tissue
structures (ie, disk, ligamentum flavum, facet capsule).
Patients with central canal stenosis typically present with neurogenic claudication.

Lumbar spine stenosis is one of the most common conditions that occurs in the elderly population.
In patients older than 65 years, spinal stenosis is the most common reason to undergo lumbar spine
surgery. Spinal stenosis is defined as a degenerative process that results in alterations in the
anatomy and mechanics of the spine. The canal may be narrowed by bony structures (ie,
osteophytosis, spondylolisthesis) or soft-tissue structures (ie, disk, ligamentum flavum, facet
capsule). Patients with central canal stenosis usually present with neurogenic claudication. Patients
with concomitant lateral recess and/or neuroforaminal stenosis may present with radiculopathy.
Epidemiology
The prevalence of lumbar spine stenosis is 20% to 25%.
Acquired stenosis may be degenerative, iatrogenic, neoplastic, or traumatic; it may be associated with
acromegaly, Paget disease, or ankylosing spondylitis.
Patients with congenital stenosis typically are symptomatic earlier in life.
The level most commonly involved is L4-L5.

Epidemiology
In a prospective study evaluating lumbar symptoms and CT findings, consisting of participants of the
Framingham Heart Study, the prevalence of lumbar spine stenosis was 23.6%.1 The prevalence of
spinal stenosis increases with age, beginning in patients in their forties. Spinal stenosis is most
commonly evident at L4-L5, and approximately 30% of patients have multilevel stenosis.2 Lumbar
spine stenosis may be acquired, congenital, or both. Acquired causes are degenerative, iatrogenic,
neoplastic, or traumatic, and may be associated with systemic conditions, such as acromegaly, Paget
disease, and ankylosing spondylitis. Patients with congenital stenosis typically present with
symptoms earlier in life, even with little evidence of lumbar spondylosis.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The canal shape may be circular, oval, or trefoil; a trefoil-shaped canal is predisposed to lateral recess
stenosis (Figure 1).
The spinal canal is separated into the central canal, lateral recess, and intervertebral foramen (Figure 2).


Anatomy and Biomechanics
The lumbar spine canal contains the thecal sac and cauda equina. The anterior boundary consists of
the intervertebral disk, vertebral body, and posterior longitudinal ligament. The lateral border
consists of the pedicles, neuroforamen, and lateral ligamentum flavum. The posterior border
consists of the facet joints, ligamentum flavum, and lamina. The spinal canal may be circular, oval, or
trefoil in shape. The spinal canal can be divided into three distinct regions: the central canal, lateral
recess, and intervertebral foramen. The central canal is bounded by the posterior longitudinal
ligament (anterior), ligamentum flavum and lamina (posterior), and medial border of the superior
articular process (lateral). The lateral recess is defined by the superior articular process (posterior),
thecal sac (medial), pedicle (lateral), and posterolateral vertebral body and lateral intervertebral disk
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Spine Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
4/23

(anterior). The intervertebral foramen is bordered by the adjacent pedicles (cranial/caudal), facet
joint and lateral ligamentum flavum (posterior), and vertebral body and intervertebral disk (anterior).
The facet (zygapophyseal) joints are encapsulated structures that have uniform cartilaginous
surfaces consisting of the superior and inferior articular process to facilitate gliding motion. Facet
tropism refers to asymmetry in facet orientation between facet joints at a given level. Facet tropism
and more sagittal facet orientation have been associated with facet degeneration and degenerative
spondylolisthesis.4 Each vertebral level is arranged as a tripod with the intervertebral disk (anterior)
flanked posteriorly by two facet joints.
The intervertebral foramen typically is larger than the ganglion and nerve that it contains. The
additional space within the foramen is occupied by fat and areolar tissue that prevent neural
compression with changes in foramen size with motion. Posterior compression within the foramen
may result from ligamentum flavum and/or facet hypertrophy. Anterior compression occurs mainly
from foraminal disk herniations but also can occur via end plate osteophytosis. Superior-inferior
compression results from loss of disk height. Loss of disk height with resultant neural compression is
important to recognize because posterior decompression alone will not afford reliable relief of
radicular complaints.
Pathophysiology
Lumbar spine stenosis is the end result of a self-propagating cycle beginning with disk degeneration and
loss of disk height that results in alterations in the structure and mechanics of the lumbar spine.
The end result of sustained neural compression is alterations in nerve root microcirculation, nerve
dysfunction, and the release of inflammatory mediators resulting in pain.

Pathophysiology
Lumbar spine stenosis results from a self-propagating degenerative cycle as theorized by Kirkaldy-
Willis et al.5-8 The degenerative cascade begins with structural changes to the disk in the form of
circumferential annular tears that result in radial annular tears. The combination of structural and
biochemical changes within in the disk result in loss of disk height that may lead to disk bulging or
frank herniation, narrowing the canal and creating the potential for neural compression. The loss of
disk height causes buckling of the ligamentum flavum and settling of the facet joints, leading to facet
deterioration and osteophytosis, further narrowing the canal and increasing the potential for neural
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Spine Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
5/23

impingement. The altered structure, motion, and mechanics within the lumbar spine culminate in
additional disk degeneration, propagating the cycle.
As the spinal canal cross-sectional area decreases, the potential for neural compression increases.
Neural compression leads to changes in function as a result of increased intraneural pressure that is
related to magnitude and the duration of compression.9-11 Increased intraneural pressure results in
microvascular congestion that interferes with neural excitability, even at low-grade sustained
compression (10 mm Hg).12-16 In addition to the direct effects of compression and the changes in
microcirculation, the local release of chemical mediators from the compressed nerve also causes
pain.17-19
Natural History
The natural history of spinal stenosis is not well understood, but it is typically favorable.

Natural History
The natural history of spinal stenosis is not well understood. In a retrospective study of patients with
asymptomatic lumbar stenosis, symptoms developed in only 23% of the patients at approximately 5
years after diagnosis. In patients with symptomatic lumbar stenosis, the natural history usually is
favorable. In a prospective study of patients with symptomatic lumbar spine stenosis who refused
surgical treatment, 70% of the patients remained unchanged, 15% improved clinically, and 15%
clinically deteriorated at a follow-up of 4 years.20 None of the patients had severe deterioration.
Cauda equina syndrome is a rare condition caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots
within the canal and may present in a delayed fashion in patients with chronic spinal stenosis.
Patients present with lower extremity weakness, perineal anesthesia, and bowel/bladder
dysfunction. Patients with congenital stenosis may have an increased risk of this condition, especially
if a superimposed disk herniation is present. Cauda equina syndrome is rarely encountered in
patients with degenerative spinal stenosis. Irrespective of etiology, if cauda equina syndrome is
diagnosed, surgical decompression should be performed as soon as possible to avoid progression of
potentially permanent neurologic deficits.21
Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
6/23

Congenital stenosis typically results in earlier presentation with little evidence of degeneration.
The trefoil-shaped spinal canal has the smallest cross-sectional area and is associated with an increased
risk of symptomatic lumbar stenosis.

Risk Factors
Congenital stenosis may be a normal anatomic variant in the population or associated with other
developmental abnormalities, such as acromegaly and achondroplasia. Congenital stenosis results
from a failure in formation of the posterior elements, resulting in short pedicles. An anatomic study
comparing patients who had congenital stenosis with age- and sex-matched control patients
reported that pedicle length was reduced by 33% and the cross-sectional area of the canal was
reduced by 34% in patients with congenital stenosis.3 These patients also had little evidence of
degenerative changes observed on MRI. A trefoil-shaped canal also predisposes an individual to
lateral recess stenosis and is present in 15% of patients.22
Classification
Anatomic classification is based on location of stenosis: central, lateral recess, foraminal.
Etiologic classification consists of acquired, congenital, or both.

Classification
Lumbar spine stenosis can be classified based on the anatomic location of stenosis: central, lateral
recess, or foraminal (Figure 3).
According to the Kirkaldy-Willis degenerative cascade,6,7 degeneration of the disk results in disk
bulging and/or frank disk herniation that decreases the cross-sectional area of the spinal canal. With
advanced degeneration, loss of disk height results in infolding and hypertrophy of the ligamentum
flavum, further decreasing the canal diameter. Neural compression by hypertrophic soft-tissue
structures is responsible for 40% of spinal stenosis.23 Lumbar flexion may re-tension the infolded
ligamentum flavum, which may temporarily increase the spinal canal diameter. The phenomenon
explains why patients with lumbar spine stenosis report improved symptoms when leaning forward
(ie, shopping cart sign). With continued deterioration, abnormal loading on the facet joints results in
facet hypertrophy, leading to canal compromise.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
7/23

Lateral recess stenosis results from disk herniation and/or facet hypertrophy. In contrast to patients
with central stenosis who present with neurogenic claudication, patients with lateral recess stenosis
present with radicular pattern symptoms—radicular pain, paresthesia, paresis—in the distribution
supplied by the affected nerve. Typically, the nerve affected is the traversing nerve root at the
affected level.
Foraminal stenosis results from loss of disk height, foraminal disk herniations, vertebral end plate
osteophytes, facet osteophytes and cysts, and spondylolisthesis. Patients with foraminal stenosis
report symptoms consistent with lumbar radiculopathy in the distribution of the exiting nerve root at
the given level. Similar to patients with central stenosis, patients with foraminal stenosis will
experience symptom exacerbation with lumbar extension, which decreases the cranial-caudal
diameter of the foramen.
Lumbar spine stenosis also is classified based on etiology, which may be acquired, congenital, or
both. Congenital stenosis is an abnormal anatomic variant in the population and is associated with
acromegaly, achondroplasia, and osteopetrosis. Acquired stenosis may be degenerative, iatrogenic,
traumatic, or associated with other systemic processes (eg, Paget disease, ankylosing spondylitis).

spondylosis with disk dehydration (arrowhead), disk protrusion (arrow), and central canal narrowing
at L2-S1. Hypertrophic changes in the ligamentum flavum and the facet joint are most prominent at
L4-S1. B, Axial T2-weighted MRI of the L4-5 interspace shows hypertrophy of the facet joint
(arrowhead) and the ligamentum flavum (arrow), causing severe central canal and lateral recess
stenosis. C, Parasagittal T1-weighted MRI shows loss of epidural fat (arrow) about the lower lumbar
exiting nerve roots (L3, L4, and L5) and neuroforaminal stenosis. (Reproduced from Issack PS,
Cunningham ME, Pumberger M, Hughes AP, Cammisa FP Jr: Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis:
Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[8]:527-535.)

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Lumbar spine stenosis is a disease of exertion, with exacerbation of symptoms with prolonged standing
and walking.
Relieving factors include lying down, sitting, and lumbar flexion (shopping cart sign).
Patients usually present with neurogenic claudication but also may report radicular complaints or a
combination.

Patient History
Patients with lumbar spine stenosis present with leg pain, typically as neurogenic claudication, with
or without radiculopathy. In a review of 68 patients with lumbar spine stenosis, neurogenic
claudication was observed in 94% of the patients and was identified as pain (93%), numbness (63%),
or subjective weakness (43%).2 Symptoms progress from proximal to distal in the leg, in contrast to
vascular claudication, which progresses from distal to proximal (small vessel to large vessel).
Prolonged walking and standing, walking down hills, and descending stairs frequently are reported
as exacerbating factors. Symptom relief is reported with sitting, lying down, and leaning forward
(shopping cart sign). Therefore, obtaining exacerbating and relieving factors from patients may aid in
the diagnosis of lumbar spine stenosis. Patients with concomitant lateral recess or foraminal
stenosis may report radicular complaints in parallel to neurogenic claudication. With concomitant
lateral recess or foraminal stenosis, patients may report symptoms at rest and may have radicular
complaints that are more prominent than neurogenic claudication.
Physical Examination
The physical examination is frequently normal in patients with spinal stenosis; however, objective findings
may be present.
A positive lumbar extension test may be indicative of lumbar spine stenosis.
A vascular examination must be performed in all patients with spinal stenosis.

Physical Examination

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
9/23

Patients typically present sitting while flexed forward on a chair in the office. On standing, patients
may assume a relatively flexed posture, with active range of motion testing revealing decreased
lumbar extension to limit or delay the onset of symptoms. Reproduction of symptoms with lumbar
extension (positive lumbar extension test) is highly predictive of lumbar spine stenosis. The
neurologic examination may be largely normal despite chronic and debilitating symptoms. Objective
neurologic findings are more common with lateral recess and/or foraminal stenosis. In a prospective
study of 100 patients with symptomatic stenosis, motor weakness was present in 23% of patients
and sensory deficit was present in 51% of patients.24
Imaging Studies
Imaging for patients in whom spinal stenosis is suspected includes plain radiography and MRI or CT
myelography.

Imaging Studies
Diagnostic evaluation typically begins with plain lumbar radiographs. Lumbar spondylosis may be
evident on radiographs. Patients with evidence of spondylolisthesis should undergo flexion and
extension radiographs to evaluate for dynamic compression. If evidence of scoliosis is present, then
long-cassette scoliosis radiographs are helpful in determining the extent of the deformity in the
coronal and sagittal planes.
MRI is the imaging modality of choice for patients in whom lumbar spine stenosis is suspected given
its ability to provide details on bony and soft-tissue anatomy. The central canal, lateral recess, and
intervertebral foramen can be inspected for the degree of stenosis. The lack of lumbar nerve root
sedimentation to the dorsal thecal sac is a positive sign of lumbar spine stenosis.25 This finding is
defined as the absence of dorsal migration of the lumbar nerve roots with the patient lying supine
while performing MRI (or CT myelography). MRI findings of stenosis are shown in Figure 4.
If MRI cannot be obtained, CT myelography can be performed to determine the extent and location
of neural compression.

Differential Diagnosis
Peripheral vascular disease, peripheral neuropathy, myelopathy, hip arthritis

Differential Diagnosis
Patients with vascular claudication (peripheral vascular disease) present with exertional pain in a
distal-to-proximal pattern (ie, small vessel to large vessel). The symptoms of vascular claudication
occur with a constant level of exertion, regardless of the lumbar spine position (negative shopping
cart sign). A bicycle stress test may help differentiate neurogenic claudication from vascular
claudication. Patients with vascular claudication will continue to experience exertion pain while
flexed forward on a bicycle. On physical examination, patients with vascular claudication will have no
pain or reproduction of symptoms with lumbar extension; may have shiny, hairless legs; and may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Spine Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
11/23

have weak peripheral pulses. The ankle-brachial index and toe-brachial index may help diagnose
peripheral vascular disease.
Patients with peripheral neuropathy may present with burning pain and dysesthesia that is
commonly reported with neurogenic claudication. A history of diabetes mellitus, nutritional
deficiencies, alcoholism, chemotherapy, and drug abuse should be obtained from these patients.
Nerve conduction studies may be useful in diagnosing peripheral neuropathy.
Patients with cord compression and myelopathy may present with the relatively vague
symptomatology without neurologic deficit that is commonly observed in patients with lumbar spine
stenosis. Tandem stenosis of the cervical and lumbar spine is known to occur with 5% to 25% neural
compression in either location.26-29 Patients with tandem stenosis may present with a complex
clinical picture of cervical stenosis (myelopathy) and lumbar stenosis; therefore, every patient
diagnosed with lumbar spine stenosis should be evaluated for concurrent cervical stenosis and
myelopathy.
Patients with hip arthritis may present with activity-related groin, buttock, and knee pain. Physical
examination revealing hip irritability and loss of internal/external rotation suggests symptomatic hip
osteoarthritis. Dedicated weight-bearing radiographs of the hip are necessary to confirm the
diagnosis of hip osteoarthritis.
Management
Overview

Overview
The decision of whether to treat patients nonsurgically or surgically must be made after considering
the degree of patient disability, the physical examination findings, and the correlative pathology.
Nonsurgical management usually is the first line of management. Surgical treatment typically is
reserved for patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails or patients with neurologic defects.
Nonsurgical Management
Drug therapy
Acetaminophen with or without NSAIDs may be used initially.

Third-generation anticonvulsants (such as gabapentin), which are used to manage neuropathic pain,
have been used in some patients with lumbar spine stenosis.
Good evidence is lacking regarding routine pharmacologic treatment in patients with spinal stenosis.
Physical therapy—No randomized controlled studies exist that define the effectiveness of physical therapy
for symptomatic lumbar spine stenosis. Regardless, a basic exercise regimen consisting of core
strengthening (abdominals and glutes) with a flexion-based lumbar stabilization program, a flexibility
regimen, and aerobic conditioning is recommended.
Epidural steroid injections

Nonsurgical Management
Medications, physical therapy, and steroid injections are mainstay of the nonsurgical management
of spinal stenosis. Medication management may include acetaminophen, NSAIDs, third-generation
anticonvulsants, and muscle relaxants. According to clinical practice guidelines from the North
American Spine Society, insufficient evidence is available to make a recommendation for or against
the use of pharmacologic treatment (Resource 1).30
NSAIDs may be effective for the short-term management of symptoms; however, NSAIDs have been
linked to increased bleeding risk and gastrointestinal and renal complications in the elderly and with
prolonged use (Resource 2).31 Third-generation anticonvulsants (eg, gabapentin) may be another
pharmacologic option. A small, randomized controlled trial of patients receiving gabapentin versus
control patients reported substantially lower visual analog pain scale scores and longer walking
tolerance in the experimental group. Adverse effects of gabapentin include sedation, which may be
synergistic with other psychotropic medications. In addition, gabapentin may be poorly tolerated in
some patients, especially the elderly.30 Opioid medications should not be used. Opioids are
associated with constipation, respiratory suppression, and changes in sensorium, especially in the
elderly population. In addition, opioids are associated with a risk for abuse.31
Similar to medications, insufficient evidence is available to make a recommendation for or against
the use of physical therapy or exercise for the management of spinal stenosis. Regardless, clinical
experience suggests that physical therapy and exercise focused on abdominal flexion exercises and
core muscle strengthening may be effective in improving outcomes.30,31
Some evidence supports the use of epidural steroid injections to provide temporary relief of
radicular symptoms and symptoms of neurogenic claudication. However, evidence regarding the
utility of epidural steroid injections for long-term benefit is mixed.30 In a prospective study of 34
patients with radicular pain caused by degenerative lumbar spine stenosis, Botwin et al32 treated

patients via fluoroscopy-guided lumbar transforaminal epidural injections. The authors reported that
75% of the patients noted at least a 50% reduction in pain scores, 64% of the patients had improved
walking tolerance, and 57% of the patients had improved standing tolerance at 1-year follow-up.
Other studies have reported only temporary improvement in pain and function after epidural
injection. Tran et al33 performed a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to examine the
nonsurgical management of lumbar spine stenosis, including the use of epidural steroid injections.
The authors determined that there may be no benefit in adding steroids to the anesthetic injection.
Clear, evidence-based guidelines regarding the number and frequency of injections needed to
manage spinal stenosis are lacking. The randomized controlled trial performed by Friedly et al34
demonstrated no benefit of steroid injections over a placebo with regard to neurogenic claudication
symptoms in patients with lumbar stenosis.
Concerns exist regarding the effects of the repetitive use of steroids on bone quality and blood
glucose levels. In patients with severe neurologic deficit, including limited walking capacity or cauda
equina syndrome, epidural steroid injections may exacerbate symptoms. In addition, case reports
have described complications, such as vascular injury, hematoma formation, and paralysis.31
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with symptoms that do not improve after a comprehensive
nonsurgical treatment regimen.
Most studies agree that, in the absence of coronal or sagittal plane deformity or segmental instability,
decompression without fusion is the appropriate surgical treatment option.
Several studies indicate that surgically treated patients experience more initial symptomatic improvement
than nonsurgically treated patients. However, initial improvements wane over time, presumably because
of progression of the degenerative process.
Convergence of outcomes between treatment groups (nonsurgical management versus surgical
management) may occur after 5 years.

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with clinical and radiographic evidence of spinal stenosis
who have intractable pain, altered quality of life, or substantially diminished functional capacity and
in whom nonsurgical treatment fails or who are not candidates for nonsurgical treatment. Surgical
treatment can predictably address positional back pain and neurogenic claudication but may not
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Spine Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001075
14/23

adequately address axial pain that may be secondary to degenerative disk disease or facet
arthropathy.31
The method of surgical treatment is based on the location and character of stenosis. Spinal stenosis
usually results from a global degenerative process that involves the central canal, lateral recesses,
neuroforamina, or a combination of these structures. Compression may be isolated or may extend
to multiple levels. Relative stability of the diseased segment also should be assessed. Segments with
evidence of instability (spondylolisthesis, lateral listhesis, or widened facets with fluid visible
observed on MRI) may require stabilization and fusion. Radicular symptoms or motor weakness
along specific nerve root distributions requires careful assessment of the lateral recess and foramen,
and may be managed via a hemilaminotomy. Neurogenic claudication with central canal stenosis
may require laminectomy or indirect reduction techniques for decompression of the central canal.
These techniques can be performed via open approaches or minimally invasive techniques.
Open laminectomy is performed with the patient in the prone position on a supportive frame that
allows the abdomen to hang free to decrease epidural venous pressure and surgical site bleeding.
Exposure of the posterior elements is performed from the midline to the lateral pars interarticularis
and facets, with great care taken to avoid damage to the facet joint capsule. After resection of the
spinous processes and the superficial dorsal lamina, central decompression is performed, with
removal of the midline laminae and underlying ligamentum flavum. Partial medial facetectomies can
then be performed to decompress the lateral recess and expose the neuroforamina and the exiting
nerve roots, which may be decompressed with the use of Kerrison rongeurs. Care is taken to
preserve the pars intra-articularis, ensuring that at least 1 cm of pars remains. A ball-tipped probe or
a Woodson elevator can be used to ensure adequate decompression of the neuroforamina31 (Figure
5).

Complications associated with laminectomy include infection, dural tear, epidural hematoma, and
instability. A study reported that after laminectomy, deep infection requiring irrigation and
débridement occurred in 2 of 103 patients (2%) with lumbar stenosis.35 Recently, a 10.5% incidence
of durotomy was reported in 389 patients who underwent laminectomy for the management of
lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis. No substantial differences in pain or physical function based
on the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form or Oswestry Disability Index scores were
observed at 1, 2, 3, and 4 years postoperatively in patients with or without durotomy, which suggests
that incidental durotomy does not substantially affect outcome.36 Epidural hematoma after
laminectomy is rare and requires urgent surgical decompression to avoid neurologic deficit. In a
study of 27 patients treated via posterior spine decompression procedures, the incidence of
postlaminectomy instability was 3.7%; this complication can be avoided by preserving the pars
interarticularis and at least 50% of the facet joints.37-39
Compared with open techniques, minimally invasive techniques for the management of spinal
stenosis result in better preservation of posterior musculature and diminished intraoperative
bleeding and require less recovery time. Minimally invasive approaches for the management of
stenosis include laminotomy through a tubular retractor, with or without a contralateral
decompression through the same hemilaminotomy. Although minimally invasive approaches are
associated with some advantages over open procedures, the economic value and cost-effectiveness
of minimally invasive techniques require additional investigation.31
Minimally invasive laminotomy involves the removal of a small portion of one side of the lamina.
Resection of the distal half of the superior hemilamina often is necessary to identify and remove the
insertion site of the ligamentum flavum. Contralateral decompression can be performed, with
preservation of the spinous processes and supraspinous and interspinous ligaments by tilting the
operating table away from the surgeon. Using an operating microscope, the contralateral
ligamentum can be visualized and resected, and then the lamina can be undercut. Accessing
stenosis in the contralateral foramen may be difficult.31
Several studies have evaluated the outcomes of decompressive laminectomy for the management of
spinal stenosis compared with those of nonsurgical management. The Maine Lumbar Spine Study
reported on the outcomes of decompressive laminectomy versus nonsurgical treatment in a cohort
of 148 patients with symptomatic lumbar stenosis who were followed for 10 years.40-42 Eighty-one
patients underwent laminectomy, and 67 patients underwent nonsurgical treatment. Both groups
were assessed at 1, 4, and 8 to 10 years after treatment. Leg or back pain was substantially improved

in 55% of patients in the surgical group and 28% of the patients in the nonsurgical group at 1-year
follow-up; however, these differences became less substantial over time. At 8- to 10-year follow-up,
leg or back pain was substantially improved in 54% of the surgically treated patients compared with
42% of the nonsurgically treated patients. These studies were limited by nonrandomized design in
which potential confounders cannot be excluded, the high rate of loss to follow-up, and various
degrees of decompression, which make assessment of the value of decompression surgery
difficult.31
More recently, prospective randomized studies have rigorously evaluated the surgical management
of spinal stenosis. Amundsen et al43 reported on the results of 100 patients with symptomatic
lumbar spine stenosis who were assigned to surgical or nonsurgical treatment. Partial randomization
was done, with 31 patients assigned to nonsurgical or surgical treatment groups. At 4-year follow-up,
excellent or fair results were observed in 9 of 18 patients in the nonsurgical group and 10 of 13
patients in the surgical group. In a randomized multicenter trial, Malmivaara et al44 evaluated 94
patients with lumbar spine stenosis who were treated surgically (50 patients) or nonsurgically (44
patients). The surgical group included 10 patients treated via instrumented posterolateral fusion. At
2-year follow-up, disability, leg pain, and back pain were improved to a greater degree in the surgical
group than in the nonsurgical group. Walking ability did not differ between the two treatment
groups. A drawback of this study is that inclusion of patients treated via fusion makes it difficult to
attribute good outcomes to decompression alone. Crossover of the patient population is another
limitation of this study; 9% of the nonsurgical group underwent surgical treatment because of
exacerbation of symptoms, and 8% of the decompressive surgery group did not undergo surgical
treatment because they experienced relief of symptoms. This further confounded the researchers’
ability to detect differences between the groups.
The effectiveness of the surgical management of lumbar spine stenosis was evaluated in the Spine
Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT) study.45-47 This prospective randomized multicenter trial
had three study arms based on diagnosis: lumbar disk herniation, degenerative spondylolisthesis, or
spinal stenosis. Patients with spinal stenosis without spondylolisthesis who had symptoms for at
least 12 weeks and in whom nonsurgical treatment failed were enrolled in the spinal stenosis arm of
the study. These patients were assigned to a randomized controlled trial or an observational cohort
and underwent decompressive surgery or nonsurgical treatment, respectively. Nonsurgical
treatment consisted of physical therapy, education and/or counseling with home exercise
instruction, and NSAIDs. Initially, 365 patients were assigned to the observational cohort; however,
many patients in the nonsurgical group opted to undergo surgical treatment. At 2-year follow-up,
193 of 289 patients (67%) in the randomized cohort had undergone surgical treatment, whereas 157
patients (43%) in the observational cohort received nonsurgical care and underwent surgical
treatment. As-treated analysis, which combined both cohorts, showed that surgical treatment was
